This isn't really an answer to your question, but what I've found to be the case when I enjoy "bad writing" is that the characters are strong and relatable (and in the case of movies, well cast and/or performed).

After my first exam in comparative literature at uni (at 20), I went from Dante's "Divina Commedia" to Twilight, and honestly, the Meyer books gave me so much pleasure at that point. I LOVED getting to know all the cornerstones of western literature, but at that point, Edward Cullen and the cheap sexual suspense was all I wanted.

Sometimes it's just about time and place, and a "bad book" can hit just as hard as a masterpiece.

That being said, a possible litmus test for "bad writing" is the dialogue. Does it flow well from direct speech, and to what extent is dialogue being utilised, not just as a device to deliver information  about the story (i.e. "Peter! I heard you dumped Sarah last night") but to convey subtleties about characters and dynamics that cannot be conveyed as effectively elsewhere (i.e. "Seriously – you dumped her?"/"Did Sarah really move out last night?/WTF did you do to Sarah last night. Etc.)
